UI pass on the Financial Resilience Engine (Storm Fund) in "/Users/ajeet/Projects/Hackathons/Sheridan Datathon 2026". HEAD 6afc283, gates green (vitest 474, typecheck 0, build PASS, pytest 160, engine verify PASS). Keep them green. React 19 / Vite 6 / TS strict / Tailwind 3.4 / Vitest.

## STAGED PROTOCOL (mandatory): each stage written to disk with green targeted tests before the next. Stages below.

## The five user notes driving this pass
1. PIXEL ART (hand-drawn, image generation is out of budget): the app must read as 2D Terraria/Stardew Valley pixel art, not a normal dashboard. Draw it as SVG/CSS (rect grids, path pixel art, image-rendering: pixelated where bitmaps appear): (a) a pixel sky header band with a DAY variant (blue sky, pixel sun, fluffy pixel clouds, distant pixel hills) and a STORM variant (indigo clouds, pixel rain streaks, pixel lightning) that swaps based on the active verdict band (storm_warning/critical -> storm, else day); (b) a small pixel mascot (smiling rain cloud over a coin jar); (c) chrome discipline: chunky 8-bit style borders (2-3px solid or stepped), hard offset shadows (no soft blur), pixel-flavored numeric readouts (keep tabular monospace, add pixel styling via letter treatment or a bundled pixel-style font ONLY if you can vendor it offline; otherwise CSS). If an empty public/art/ dir exists from failed image jobs, remove it. Quality bar: deliberate chunky pixels on a visible grid (each pixel a consistent unit), limited retro palette that still works on the light theme; no mushy anti-aliased gradients pretending to be pixel art.
2. CARTOGRAM AS A REAL MAP: district tiles must become an actual map of Czechia. districts.csv has no coordinates; fetch public domain Czechia district (okresy, 77 incl. Praha) GeoJSON at BUILD time (network allowed now, runtime stays offline), simplify to SVG paths (target: whole file under ~150 KB; Douglas-Peucker or pre-simplified source), name-match all 77 districts to districts.csv district_name (normalize: strip prefixes, handle "Hl.m. Praha"/"Hlavní město Praha" -> Praha, diacritics). Render one <path> per district shaded by the district's verdict-band share from the existing atlas.json contract (do not change the data contract; read src/lib/atlasData.ts and Cartogram.tsx first). Commit the simplified geometry into the repo (src/assets or public/data) so runtime never fetches it. Keep/handle no_data districts visibly. Update Cartogram.test.ts (and probe.test.tsx if affected) for path rendering while preserving existing coverage intent (77 districts, shading values, click/hover behavior). Report any unmatched districts with a tile fallback and list them.
3. LAYOUT ORDER: judges must reach the account entry first. src/App.tsx currently mounts <section id="atlas"> ABOVE <div id="console">. Swap: console FIRST (its internal order already is lookup -> baseline+shock -> forecast -> plan, which is what the user wants: "Know the customer, Current conditions, Take a shock to the top, forecast"), atlas section AFTER the console, JudgeBar stays sticky bottom. Keep both ids, keep scroll-to-console behavior working (dot click scrolls to #console which is now above; verify no jarring reverse scroll), update any test asserting order (app.smoke etc.).
4. GEMINI KEY: local demo only (user confirmed; do NOT touch .github workflows). The local .env already holds the key. Improve the typed-shock fallback copy so a "key not configured" state explains: typed shocks run on a local build (npm run dev or build and preview with .env); the deployed build falls back to preset cards. Keep the failure honest and short, no key hints. Verify locally WITHOUT printing the key: build and confirm the key is embedded (e.g. node -e script that checks the built asset contains a non-empty VITE_GEMINI_KEY value by length only; never echo it).
5. LIGHT THEME: convert from the near-black ground to a light, readable, daylight-weather palette. Scope: the cp- tokens (src/index.css), wx- (weather.css), ax- (atlas.css), jg- (judge.css), tailwind.config.js colors, and any component-level hardcoded dark colors (grep for #070c18, #0d1526, #e9effa, rgba(0,0 etc.). Direction: soft daylight (think morning forecast map on paper: off-white/very pale sky-tinted backgrounds, dark slate text), panels as white cards with the chunky pixel borders, the five band hues KEPT as accents but re-tuned for AA contrast on light ground (critical stays hot, storm amber darkened for text-on-light, watch purple, fair blue, clear green; glyphs/icons keep redundant encoding). The pixel sky header reads best as the color source; keep data density readable. Do NOT fall into the generic cream+serif+terracotta look: this is a pixel game weather station in daylight. Respect prefers-reduced-motion, focus-visible, and keep every verdict color paired with glyph+label (never color alone). Contrast: spot-check body text and band labels against their new backgrounds (report ratios).

## HARD CONSTRAINTS
- Integer cents, zero money math in components, single band vocabulary src/lib/verdict.ts (do not reintroduce the seven-state ladder).
- NO em/en dashes, minus sign equivalents, double or spaced hyphens in ANY new string/comment/CSS prose (dashScan.test.ts must stay green and may need new files registered).
- Runtime offline: only bundled fetches (profiles.json, atlas.json); the GeoJSON is build-time only.
- Do NOT touch: scripts/engine/*, scripts/analysis/*, docs/devpost.md, docs/video/*, README.md, .github/*, consoleStore behavior (comments only if needed), judge key semantics.
- If you must change tests to reflect intentional UI changes, update assertions rather than deleting coverage; keep the suite honest.

## STAGES (suggested order)
1. Light theme token rework (index.css, tailwind, the four style files, hardcoded color sweep) + run full vitest (colors are mostly structural in tests; fix fallout).
2. App layout swap + order-dependent test updates.
3. Pixel art assets: pixel sky header (day/storm swap on active band), mascot, chrome pass (borders/shadows/readouts) + new component tests (day/storm swap logic pinned).
4. Cartogram real map: fetch + simplify + name-match + path rendering + tests (all 77 districts accounted for; unmatched listed).
5. Gemini fallback copy + build-time key verification + dashScan registration for any new files + FULL GATES: npx vitest run, npm run typecheck, npm run build, uv run pytest -q, uv run python -m scripts.engine.verify.

## Report
Files per stage; name-match results (77/77 or the fallback list); geometry source URL + final size; contrast ratios for band labels; day/storm swap rule; key-embedded verification (length only); all gate outputs; deviations with rationale.

If you need clarification or encounter ambiguity, output your questions in this exact format at the TOP of your response:

## QUESTIONS FOR USER
- Q1: [your question]

Then continue with your best-effort output based on available information.

<skill_content name="frontend-design">
# Skill: frontend-design

# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for giving every client a visual identity that could not be mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take one real aesthetic risk you can justify.

## Ground it in the subject

If the brief does not pin down what the product or subject is, pin it yourself before designing: name one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job, and state your choice. If there's any information in your memory about the human's preferences, context about what they're building, or designs you've made before – use that as a hint. The subject's own world, its materials, instruments, artifacts, and vernacular, is where distinctive choices come from. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is a thesis. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in whatever form makes sense for it: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the template answer, only use if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Structure is information. Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated.

Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: brainstorm, explore, plan, critique, build, critique again

For calibration: AI-generated design right now clusters around three looks: (1) a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta accent; (2) a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent; (3) a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns. All three are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. Just like a human designer who's hired, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the human's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and signature. Color: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values. Type: the typefaces for 2+ roles (a characterful display face that's used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed). Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Signature: the single unique element this page will be remembered by that embodies the brief in an appropriate way.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan exactly and deriving every color and type decision from it.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and a element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with paddings/margins between sections.

Try to do a lot of this planning and iteration in your thinking, and only show ideas to the user when you have higher confidence it'll delight them.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let the signature element be the one memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Not taking a risk can be a risk itself! Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots if your environment supports it – a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creators have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand, and therefore easier to use. They are design material, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality to copy that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's side of the screen. Name things by what people control and recognize, never by how the system is built. A person manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A control should say exactly what happens when it's used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the register conversational and tuned: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each element do exactly one job. A label labels, an example demonstrates, and nothing quietly does double duty.

Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan exactly and deriving every color and type decision from it.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and a element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with paddings/margins between sections.

Try to do a lot of this planning and iteration in your thinking, and only show ideas to the user when you have higher confidence it'll delight them.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let the signature element be the one memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Not taking a risk can be a risk itself! Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots if your environment supports it – a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creators have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand, and therefore easier to use. They are design material, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality to copy that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's side of the screen. Name things by what people control and recognize, never by how the system is built. A person manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A control should say exactly what happens when it's used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the register conversational and tuned: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each element do exactly one job. A label labels, an example demonstrates, and nothing quietly does double duty.

444: /**

446:  * land in the critical or storm_warning bands, as a fraction from 0

453:   const total = bandTotal(counts)

483:   { bin: 2, band: 'watch', range: 'over 5 to 15%' },

170: /** Refuse any extra or missing key so the contract cannot silently grow. */
171: function requireExactKeys(record: RawRecord, expected: readonly string[], name: string): void {
172:   const actual = Object.keys(record)
173:   const missing = expected.filter((key) => !actual.includes(key))
174:   const extra = actual.filter((key) => !expected.includes(key))
175:   if (missing.length > 0 || extra.length > 0) {
176:     const parts: string[] = []
177:     if (missing.length > 0) {

179:     }
180:     if (extra.length > 0) {
181:       parts.push(`unexpected ${extra.join(', ')}`)

192:  * code, logs, and docs. The guarantee is scoped to the band list

197:   const hasVerdictBands = Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(root, 'verdict_bands')

199:   if (hasVerdictBands && hasStates) {
200:     throw new Error('atlas.json must carry one band list key, verdict_bands or states, not both')
201:   }
202:   if (hasVerdictBands) {
203:     return 'verdict_bands'

211: function parseBandList(raw: unknown, name: string): VerdictBandId[] {
212:   const list = asArray(raw, name)

216:   for (let index = 0; index < ATLAS_BAND_IDS.length; index += 1) {

225:   const record = asRecord(raw, name)

227:   const counts = {} as BandCounts
228:   for (const band of ATLAS_BAND_IDS) {
229:     counts[band] = asCount(record[band], `${name}.${band}`)

235:   const sources = asArray(raw, 'sources')
236:   return sources.map((entry, index) => {
237:     const name = `sources[${index}]`
238:     const record = asRecord(entry, name)
239:     requireExactKeys(record, SOURCE_KEYS, name)
240:     const rows = asCount(record.rows, `${name}.rows`)

249: function parseDistricts(raw: unknown): DistrictRow[] {
250:   const rows = asArray(raw, 'districts')
251:   const seen = new Set<number>()
252:   return rows.map((entry, index) => {
253:     const name = `districts[${index}]`
254:     const record = asRecord(entry, name)
255:     requireExactKeys(record, DISTRICT_KEYS, name)
256:     const districtId = asCount(record.district_id, `${name}.district_id`)
257:     if (seen.has(districtId)) {
258:       throw new Error(`${name}.district_id must be unique, got ${districtId} twice`)
259:     }
260:     seen.add(districtId)
261:     const accountCount = asCount(record.account_count, `${name}.account_count`)
262:     return {
263:       district_id: districtId,
264:       district_name: asString(record.district_name, `${name}.district_name`),
265:       region: asString(record.region, `${name}.region`),
266:       inhabitants: asCount(record.inhabitants, `${name}.inhabitants`),
267:       unemployment_rate_2023: asFiniteNumberOrNull(
268:         record.unemployment_rate_2023,
269:         `${name}.unemployment_rate_2023`,
270:       ),
271:       average_salary: asFiniteNumberOrNull(record.average_salary, `${name}.average_salary`),
272:       account_count: accountCount,
273:       no_data: asBoolean(record.no_data, `${name}.no_data`),

278: /**
279:  * Every account map value must name a district that exists, and each
280:  * district must be mapped exactly account_count times, so the map and
281:  * the district table can never disagree about how many accounts live
282:  * where.
283:  */
284: function parseAccountDistrict(
285:   raw: unknown,
286:   districts: readonly DistrictRow[],
287: ): Record<string, number> {
288:   const record = asRecord(raw, 'account_district')
289:   const byDistrict = new Map(districts.map((row) => [row.district_id, row]))
290:   const mapped = new Map<number, number>()
291:   for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(record)) {
292:     if (!ACCOUNT_ID_PATTERN.test(key)) {
293:       throw new Error(`account_district key "${key}" must be an account id of digits`)
294:     }
295:     const districtId = asCount(value, `account_district["${key}"]`)
296:     if (!byDistrict.has(districtId)) {
297:       throw new Error(`account_district["${key}"] must name a district in districts, got ${districtId}`)
298:     }
299:     mapped.set(districtId, (mapped.get(districtId) ?? 0) + 1)
300:   }
301:   for (const row of districts) {
302:     const count = mapped.get(row.district_id) ?? 0
303:     if (count !== row.account_count) {
304:       throw new Error(
305:         `account_district maps ${count} accounts to district ${row.district_id}, expected districts account_count ${row.account_count}`,
306:       )

308:   }
309:   return record as Record<string, number>

312: /**
313:  * A district split table: keys exactly the district ids, each counts
314:  * object exactly the five bands, each object summing to its district
315:  * account_count. Used for baseline and for every scenario.
316:  */

318:   raw: unknown,
319:   name: string,
320:   districts: readonly DistrictRow[],
321: ): Record<string, BandCounts> {
322:   const record = asRecord(raw, name)
323:   const expected = districts.map((row) => String(row.district_id))
324:   requireExactKeys(record, expected, name)
325:   const out: Record<string, BandCounts> = {}
326:   for (const key of expected) {
327:     const counts = parseBandCounts(record[key], `${name}[${key}]`)
328:     const district = districts.find((row) => String(row.district_id) === key) as DistrictRow
329:     const total = bandTotal(counts)
330:     if (total !== district.account_count) {
331:       throw new Error(
332:         `${name}[${key}] band counts sum to ${total}, expected districts account_count ${district.account_count}`,
333:       )
334:     }
335:     out[key] = counts
336:   }
337:   return out

340: /**
341:  * Exactly the four shipped preset tables: the module doc and both
342:  * Python gates (verify.py, test_atlas.py) treat the full set as fixed
343:  * contract, so a trimmed artifact is refused here with the missing
344:  * ids named instead of silently falling back to baseline tiles, and an
345:  * invented preset id keeps its own refusal.
346:  */
347: function parseScenarios(
348:   raw: unknown,
349:   districts: readonly DistrictRow[],
350: ): Record<string, Record<string, BandCounts>> {
351:   const record = asRecord(raw, 'scenarios')
352:   const actual = new Set(Object.keys(record))
353:   for (const presetId of actual) {
354:     if (!PRESET_IDS.has(presetId)) {
355:       throw new Error(`scenarios key "${presetId}" is not a shipped shock preset id`)
356:     }

359:   if (missing.length > 0) {

361:       `scenarios must carry all four shipped preset tables, missing ${missing.join(', ')}`,
362:     )
363:   }
364:   const out: Record<string, Record<string, BandCounts>> = {}
365:   for (const [presetId, value] of Object.entries(record)) {
366:     out[presetId] = parseDistrictCounts(value, `scenarios[${presetId}]`, districts)

368:   return out

371: /**
372:  * Validate a parsed atlas.json payload against the fixed schema and
373:  * index nothing: the artifact is already keyed the way the UI reads
374:  * it. Every refusal names the field that broke the contract.
375:  */
376: export function parseAtlasDoc(raw: unknown): AtlasDoc {
377:   const root = asRecord(raw, 'atlas.json')
378:   const bandKey = pickBandListKey(root)
379:   requireExactKeys(
380:     root,
381:     ['schema_version', 'generated_by', bandKey, 'sources', 'districts', 'account_district', 'baseline', 'scenarios'],

394:     schema_version: schemaVersion,
395:     generated_by: asString(root.generated_by, 'generated_by'),
396:     verdict_bands: parseBandList(root[bandKey], bandKey),
397:     sources: parseSources(root.sources),
398:     districts,
399:     account_district: parseAccountDistrict(root.account_district, districts),
400:     baseline: parseDistrictCounts(root.baseline, 'baseline', districts),
401:     scenarios: parseScenarios(root.scenarios, districts),
402:   }
403: }

405: /** Fetch and validate the bundled atlas artifact (one bundled file). */
406: export async function loadAtlas(): Promise<AtlasDoc> {
407:   const response = await fetch(`${dataBase()}data/engine/atlas.json`)
408:   if (!response.ok) {
409:     throw new Error(`atlas.json fetch failed with status ${response.status}`)

416:  * pattern as loadSharedProfiles, one request and one parse per boot
417:  * and no external network. A failed load clears the memo so the next
418:  * boot retries instead of inheriting the rejection forever.

432: /**

434:  * counts, used for every share this file and its callers print.
435:  */
436: export function bandTotal(counts: BandCounts): number {
437:   let total = 0
438:   for (const band of ATLAS_BAND_IDS) {
439:     total += counts[band]

441:   return total
442: }

444: /**
445:  * District severity: the share of a district's counted accounts that
446:  * land in the critical or storm_warning bands, as a fraction from 0
447:  * to 1. This is the definition the cartogram legend prints (see
448:  * SEVERITY_DEFINITION): one number, two bands, denominator is the
449:  * district's own account total. A district with no accounts to count
450:  * reports 0, and callers must pass counts, never recompute them.
451:  */

453:   const total = bandTotal(counts)
454:   if (total <= 0) {

456:   }
457:   return (counts.critical + counts.storm_warning) / total

460: /** One shading bin: 0 is no severity, 4 is the heaviest. */
461: export type SeverityBin = 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4

463: export interface SeverityBinSpec {
464:   bin: SeverityBin

466:   band: VerdictBandId

468:   range: string

471: /**

473:  * the five band colors in ladder order: a district with nothing in
474:  * the two risk bands reads Clear, the heaviest district reads
475:  * Critical. The thresholds sit low on purpose because a baseline
476:  * population spends most of its districts near zero, so a preset
477:  * twist has somewhere visible to cascade into. Bin 0 is exactly zero;
478:  * every other bin is a half open interval written as percent words.
479:  */
480: export const SEVERITY_BINS: readonly SeverityBinSpec[] = [
481:   { bin: 0, band: 'clear', range: 'exactly 0%' },
482:   { bin: 1, band: 'fair_skies', range: 'over 0 to 5%' },
483:   { bin: 2, band: 'watch', range: 'over 5 to 15%' },
484:   { bin: 3, band: 'storm_warning', range: 'over 15 to 40%' },
485:   { bin: 4, band: 'critical', range: 'over 40%' },

504:   if (share <= 0.4) {

506:   }

508: }

- `--rp-void` → light ground: `#eef3fb` (pale sky-tinted paper) — actually let's name:
  - **Daylight ground** `#e8eef8` (very pale sky blue paper)
  - **Panel white** `#ffffff`
  - **Ink (slate)** `#1e2a3d` (dark slate text)
  - **Ink dim** `#4a5a72`
  - **Rule** `#93a4c0` (border) — needs enough contrast for borders; borders aren't text so lower contrast fine but let's use `#8497b5`.
  
Band hues re-tuned for AA on light:
 - critical (hot): `#c62d10`? Need contrast on white ≥ 4.5 for text. Let's compute later. Current `#ff6a4d` on white = poor (about 3.0). For text-on-light we need darker: `#c22e10` or `#b52c12`.
  - storm amber darkened: `#a15c00`? Amber `#f4b740` on white ~1.9. Darker `#8a5a00`.
  - watch purple: `#8b7cf6` on white ~2.9; darker `#5b4bd6`?
  - fair blue: `#39c2e0` → `#0b6f92`?  - clear green: `#35d0ae` → `#0d7a5f`?

Hmm, but these band colors are used both as text colors and as fills (swatches, left rules, glyph colors, map shading). For map shading we want lighter fills. Two-tier: `--cp-band-*` for text/accents (dark enough for AA), and a fill variant for shading (lighter). Actually the existing design uses `--cp-band-*` for both text (via tailwind text-cp-*) and fills (data-band mapping, ax-tile background color-mix). Since the map shading uses `color-mix(in srgb, var(--ax-band) 22%, var(--cp-surface))`, a darker band color at 22% still reads fine.

But wait — glyphs are large text (clamp 2-3.25rem) which needs only 3:1 contrast (large text). Band labels `.cp-verdict__label` at clamp(1.125rem..1.5rem) bold — bold ≥14pt(18.66px)... Actually large-scale text = 18pt (24px) normal or 14pt (18.66px) bold. `.cp-verdict__label` is font-weight 700, font-size clamp1.125rem = 18px at min... 18px < 18.66px, so technically not "large text" at the smallest size. So band labels need 4.5:1 ideally.

Let's aim: band text colors ≥ 4.5:1 against both white panel and the pale ground.

Let me pick candidates and compute contrast ratios with a script later.

- Ground: `#eaf1fa` (pale sky paper)
- Panel: `#ffffff`
- Panel inset (was rgba dark): `#e3ebf7` (slightly deeper tint)
- Ink: `#17263b` (dark slate)
- Ink dim: `#41546f`
- Ink faint: `#64748f` (need ≥4.5 for small text... `#64748f` on white ≈ 4.6? let's compute)
- Rule: `#8fa3c2` / `#7b8fae`
- Signal (header title): a blue that works on pale ground: `#0d6ea8`?
- Verified teal: `#0d7a5f`
- Money amber: `#8a5a00`
- Stamp red: `#c22e10`

Band hues (text-safe):
- critical `#c22e10`
- storm `#9a5b00` (dark amber)
- watch `#5f4bd0`
- fair `#0b6d94`
- clear `#0b7a5e`

Hmm but "the five band hues KEPT as accents but re-tuned for AA contrast on light ground (critical stays hot, storm amber darkened for text-on-light, watch purple, fair blue, clear green". Yes exactly this direction.

But there's a catch: band colors are also used as *fill* colors for glyphs (weather glyphs like ⛈🌧☁⛅☀) and for map shading and swatches. Darker versions are fine.

Also `.wx-slot` uses fill-opacity 0.22 with currentColor — a dark band at 0.22 opacity on white gives a pale tint. Good.

`.ax-seg` opacity 0.09, `.ax-bar` 0.4, `.ax-dot` 0.75 — on white these will read OK with darker colors.

`.wx-band-active` box-shadow inset 0 0 0 2px var(--wx-parchment) — parchment is light; on light background the active ring should be dark ink instead.

`.wx-pin__label` has stroke var(--wx-grounds) with fill parchment — on light grounds, the label should be dark text with white stroke. So `--wx-parchment` becomes dark ink, and `--wx-grounds` becomes light. Wait: `--wx-parchment: #e9e0c9` used for text; `--wx-grounds: #070c18` used as background and as the stroke halo behind text on the strip. In the light theme: `--wx-grounds` → light (e.g. `#ffffff` or the pale ground), `--wx-parchment` → dark ink. Then `.wx-pin__label` fill = dark ink, stroke = light → halo works. And `.wx-cliff__label` background = var(--wx-storm) with color var(--wx-grounds) → amber bg with light text — needs dark text: color should be white/void... hmm `--wx-grounds` would be light so text on storm amber would be light-on-amber = bad. Let me instead set `--wx-grounds` to the page ground (light) and for `.wx-cliff__label` set color to a specific dark or white value.

Careful: `.wx-pin-dot` stroke: var(--wx-grounds) → light stroke around a colored dot on a light strip: fine (separates dot from line).

`.wx-band-active` inset ring var(--wx-parchment) → dark ring. Good.

`.wx-cliff__label` background var(--wx-storm) color var(--wx-grounds): with storm = dark amber `#9a5b00` and grounds = light `#eef4fc`, contrast of light text on dark amber... `#eef4fc` on `#9a5b00`: amber luminance is lowish. Probably ~4.5+. Let's compute. Alternatively use white text explicitly.

Hmm, actually maybe better: keep the cliff label background as the amber with white text (like a warning chip). I'll compute.

OK. Rather than agonizing, let me write a contrast calculator script (node) to verify ratios as I go. That's the honest approach: report ratios.

**Pixel art header**: 
- A `<header>` band rendered as SVG with a visible pixel grid. Day variant: blue sky gradient? No — "no mushy anti-aliased gradients pretending to be pixel art". So use discrete bands of flat color: sky as a few horizontal flat bands (like a 4-step sky), pixel sun (square/plus-shaped), fluffy pixel clouds (rect clusters), distant pixel hills (stepped rects), maybe a ground line.
- Storm variant: indigo cloud bands, pixel rain streaks (diagonal 1px rects), pixel lightning (stepped polygon).
- Each pixel = a consistent unit (e.g., 8px viewBox units with `shape-rendering: crispEdges`).

Signature element: the pixel sky header that changes with the verdict band.

**Mascot**: small pixel mascot — smiling rain cloud over a coin jar. SVG rect grid, ~64x48 px, `shape-rendering: crispEdges`, `image-rendering: pixelated` not needed for pure SVG but we can use `image-rendering: pixelated` on any bitmap. There are no bitmaps. We'll draw with rects on a grid.

Where does the mascot go? In the header next to the title, maybe. Good.

**Chrome discipline**: chunky 8-bit borders (2-3px solid), hard offset shadows (no soft blur), pixel numeric readouts.

So `.cp-panel` gets `border: 2px solid var(--cp-rule)` + `box-shadow: 4px 4px 0 0 var(--cp-shadow)`. Buttons get borders + hard shadows too.

Careful: the Cartogram stylesheet test asserts every `transition:` in atlas.css is inside a no-preference gate. Adding box-shadow won't break. But if I add transitions to index.css... no test asserts that for index.css? Let me check: there might be a test asserting index.css reduced motion. Let me grep tests for `prefers-reduced-motion`.

Also there's `ReceiptStamp.test.ts`, `JudgeBar.test.ts` etc. that may assert CSS content. Let me grep tests reading CSS files.

import { blocks, type Px } from './pixelGrid'

/**
 * The station mascot: a smiling rain cloud over a coin jar, drawn on the
 * same 32 by 32 unit grid as the sky band so the two share one pixel
 * size. Every shape is outlined in one unit of slate ink, which is what
 * lets the mascot read on the pale day sky and on the indigo storm sky
 * alike. It is decorative company for the title, so it is aria hidden.
 */

/** Cloud silhouette: three steps up plus one shaded underside row. */
const CLOUD: Px[] = [
  [9, 2, 10, 3, '#ffffff'],
  [6, 5, 16, 4, '#ffffff'],
  [4, 9, 20, 4, '#ffffff'],
  [4, 13, 20, 1, '#d8ecff'],
]

/** The same silhouette grown by one unit, drawn first as the outline. */
const CLOUD_INK: Px[] = [
  [8, 1, 12, 5, '#16273f'],
  [5, 4, 18, 6, '#16273f'],
  [3, 8, 22, 6, '#16273f'],
  [3, 12, 22, 3, '#16273f'],
]

/** Two eyes and a three block smile. */
const FACE: Px[] = [
  [9, 6, 2, 2, '#16273f'],
  [17, 6, 2, 2, '#16273f'],
  [10, 10, 1, 1, '#16273f'],
  [19, 10, 1, 1, '#16273f'],
  [11, 11, 7, 1, '#16273f'],
]

/** Three drips, each an outlined pixel column. */
const DRIPS: Px[] = [
  [8, 14, 3, 6, '#16273f'],
  [14, 14, 3, 6, '#16273f'],
  [20, 14, 3, 6, '#16273f'],
  [9, 15, 1, 4, '#7fc3ff'],
  [15, 15, 1, 4, '#7fc3ff'],
  [21, 15, 1, 4, '#7fc3ff'],
]

/** Jar: ink shell, pale glass, gold lid, three square coins. */
const JAR: Px[] = [
  [6, 20, 20, 12, '#16273f'],
  [7, 21, 18, 11, '#e8f1fc'],
  [7, 21, 18, 3, '#ffd23f'],
  [9, 26, 5, 3, '#ffb42e'],
  [16, 25, 5, 3, '#ffb42e'],
  [12, 29, 6, 3, '#ffb42e'],
]

/** Draw order: outline under fill, cloud over drips over jar. */
const MASCOT: Px[] = [...CLOUD_INK, ...CLOUD, ...FACE, ...DRIPS, ...JAR]

export default function PixelMascot() {
  return (
    <svg
      className="px-mascot"
      viewBox="0 0 32 32"
      width="64"
      height="64"
      shapeRendering="crispEdges"
      aria-hidden="true"
      focusable="false"
    >
      {blocks(MASCOT, 'mascot')}
    </svg>
  )
}

import { blocks, type Px } from './pixelGrid'

/**
 * The station mascot: a smiling rain cloud over a coin jar, drawn on the
 * same 32 by 32 unit grid as the sky band so the two share one pixel
 * size. Every shape is outlined in one unit of slate ink, which is what
 * lets the mascot read on the pale day sky and on the indigo storm sky
 * alike. It is decorative company for the title, so it is aria hidden.
 */

/** Cloud silhouette: three steps up plus one shaded underside row. */
const CLOUD: Px[] = [
  [9, 2, 10, 3, '#ffffff'],
  [6, 5, 16, 4, '#ffffff'],
  [4, 9, 20, 4, '#ffffff'],
  [4, 13, 20, 1, '#d8ecff'],
]

/** The same silhouette grown by one unit, drawn first as the outline. */
const CLOUD_INK: Px[] = [
  [8, 1, 12, 5, '#16273f'],
  [5, 4, 18, 6, '#16273f'],
  [3, 8, 22, 6, '#16273f'],
  [3, 12, 22, 3, '#16273f'],
]

/** Two eyes and a three block smile. */
const FACE: Px[] = [
  [9, 6, 2, 2, '#16273f'],
  [17, 6, 2, 2, '#16273f'],
  [10, 10, 1, 1, '#16273f'],
  [19, 10, 1, 1, '#16273f'],
  [11, 11, 7, 1, '#16273f'],
]

/** Three drips, each an outlined pixel column. */
const DRIPS: Px[] = [
  [8, 14, 3, 6, '#16273f'],
  [14, 14, 3, 6, '#16273f'],
  [20, 14, 3, 6, '#16273f'],
  [9, 15, 1, 4, '#7fc3ff'],
  [15, 15, 1, 4, '#7fc3ff'],
  [21, 15, 1, 4, '#7fc3ff'],
]

/** Jar: ink shell, pale glass, gold lid, three square coins. */
const JAR: Px[] = [
  [6, 20, 20, 12, '#16273f'],
  [7, 21, 18, 11, '#e8f1fc'],
  [7, 21, 18, 3, '#ffd23f'],
  [9, 26, 5, 3, '#ffb42e'],
  [16, 25, 5, 3, '#ffb42e'],
  [12, 29, 6, 3, '#ffb42e'],
]

/** Draw order: outline under fill, cloud over drips over jar. */
const MASCOT: Px[] = [...CLOUD_INK, ...CLOUD, ...FACE, ...DRIPS, ...JAR]

export default function PixelMascot() {
  return (
    <svg
      className="px-mascot"
      viewBox="0 0 32 32"
      width="64"
      height="64"
      shapeRendering="crispEdges"
      aria-hidden="true"
      focusable="false"
    >
      {blocks(MASCOT, 'mascot')}
    </svg>
  )
}

1. `skyVariantFor` rule pinned (pure): null → day, clear/fair/watch → day, storm_warning/critical → storm.

But `vi.unstubAllGlobals()` in afterEach removes the fetch stub; the memoized bundle persists ✓.

```ts

import { URL as NodeURL } from 'node:url'
import { act, createElement } from 'react'

import PixelSky, { skyVariantFor } from './PixelSky'
import { useConsole } from '../../state/consoleStore'

;(globalThis as { IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT?: boolean }).IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT = true

let mounted: { container: HTMLElement; root: Root } | null = null

afterEach(() => { ... unmount ...; vi.unstubAllGlobals() })

function stubBundledData(): void { ... }

async function renderSky(): Promise<HTMLElement> {...}

async function untilVariant(container, variant): Promise<void> { poll for svg[data-variant=variant] }

async function settle(): Promise<void> { act with a tick }
```

For driving the store, I can call `useConsole.getState()` actions inside `act`:

```ts
await act(async () => {
  await useConsole.getState().boot()
})
await act(async () => {
  useConsole.getState().selectAccount('68257')
})
```

Since PixelSky subscribes via useConsole, state updates trigger re-render ✓.

Test flow:
```ts
it('stays day until an account carries a band', async () => {
  stubBundledData()
  const container = await renderSky()
  expect(variantOf(container)).toBe('day')

  await act(async () => { await useConsole.getState().boot() })
  await act(async () => { useConsole.getState().selectAccount('68257') })
  //68257 baseline is Fair skies, so the sky stays day.
  expect(variantOf(container)).toBe('day')

  await act(async () => { useConsole.getState().applyPreset('combo') })
  // combo lands Storm warning, the storm scene takes over.
  expect(variantOf(container)).toBe('storm')

  await act(async () => { useConsole.getState().applyPreset('emergency_repair') })
  expect(variantOf(container)).toBe('storm')

  await act(async () => { useConsole.getState().resetTwist() })
  expect(variantOf(container)).toBe('day')

  await act(async () => { useConsole.getState().resetAll() })
  expect(variantOf(container)).toBe('day')
})
```

"""Build-time geometry step for the district cartogram.

Fetches nothing (the GeoJSON is downloaded separately), projects the
Czechia district outlines to a flat map, simplifies them with
Douglas-Peucker, and writes src/assets/czechia-districts.ts as plain
SVG path data. Runtime never sees this file's inputs: the app imports
the emitted module directly.

Usage: python3 build_district_map.py <input.geojson> <output.ts> <tolerance>
"""

import json
import math
import sys
import unicodedata
import re


def project(lon, lat, lat0, lon0):
    return ((lon - lon0) * math.cos(math.radians(lat0)), -lat)


def rings_of(geometry):
    if geometry["type"] == "Polygon":
        return geometry["coordinates"]
    out = []
    for poly in geometry["coordinates"]:
        out.extend(poly)
    return out


def simplify(points, tolerance):
    """Iterative Douglas-Peucker over a closed ring (first == last)."""
    if len(points) < 5:
        return points
    keep = [False] * len(points)
    keep[0] = keep[-1] = True
    stack = [(0, len(points) - 1)]
    tol2 = tolerance * tolerance
    while stack:
        start, end = stack.pop()
        if end <= start + 1:
            continue
        ax, ay = points[start]
        bx, by = points[end]
        dx, dy = bx - ax, by - ay
        norm = dx * dx + dy * dy
        best = -1.0
        best_i = -1
        for i in range(start + 1, end):
            px, py = points[i]
            if norm == 0:
                d = (px - ax) ** 2 + (py - ay) ** 2
            else:
                t = ((px - ax) * dx + (py - ay) * dy) / norm
                t = 0.0 if t < 0 else (1.0 if t > 1 else t)
                cx, cy = ax + t * dx, ay + t * dy
                d = (px - cx) ** 2 + (py - cy) ** 2
            if d > best:
                best = d
                best_i = i
        if best > tol2 and best_i > 0:
            keep[best_i] = True
            stack.append((start, best_i))
            stack.append((best_i, end))
    return [p for p, k in zip(points, keep) if k]


def normalize(name):
    text = "".join(
        c for c in unicodedata.normalize("NFD", name) if not unicodedata.combining(c)
    )
    text = re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", " ", text.lower()).strip()
    tokens = text.split()
    prefix = {"hl", "hlavni", "mesto", "m"}
    while len(tokens) > 1 and tokens[0] in prefix:
        tokens = tokens[1:]
    tokens = ["nad" if t == "n" else t for t in tokens]
    return " ".join(tokens)


# geoBoundaries ships English names for nine city and direction units.
ALIASES = {
    "prague": "praha",
    "prague east": "praha vychod",
    "prague west": "praha zapad",
    "plzen city": "plzen mesto",
    "plzen north": "plzen sever",
    "plzen south": "plzen jih",
    "brno city": "brno mesto",
    "brno country": "brno venkov",
    "ostrava city": "ostrava mesto",
}


def key_for(name):
    key = normalize(name)
    return ALIASES.get(key, key)


def main():
    src_path, out_path, tolerance = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], float(sys.argv[3])
    doc = json.load(open(src_path, encoding="utf-8"))

    # Project everything once so the tolerance is isotropic on the map.
    lats, lons = [], []
    for feature in doc["features"]:
        for ring in rings_of(feature["geometry"]):
            for lon, lat in ring:
                lons.append(lon)
                lats.append(lat)
    lat0 = (min(lats) + max(lats)) / 2
    lon0 = (min(lons) + max(lons)) / 2

    projected = []
    for feature in doc["features"]:
        shape = []
        for ring in rings_of(feature["geometry"]):
            pts = [project(lon, lat, lat0, lon0) for lon, lat in ring]
            pts = simplify(pts, tolerance)
            if len(pts) >= 4:
                shape.append(pts)
        projected.append((feature["properties"]["shapeName"], shape))

    xs = [p[0] for _, shape in projected for ring in shape for p in ring]
    ys = [p[1] for _, shape in projected for ring in shape for p in ring]
    min_x, max_x, min_y, max_y = min(xs), max(xs), min(ys), max(ys)

    # Fit a 1000 wide viewBox, keep the real aspect, pad the border.
    pad = 6.0
    span_x = max_x - min_x
    span_y = max_y - min_y
    width = 1000.0
    height = round(width * span_y / span_x)
    scale = (width - 2 * pad) / span_x

    def emit(points):
        steps = []
        for x, y in points:
            sx = round((x - min_x) * scale + pad)
            sy = round((y - min_y) * scale + pad)
            steps.append(f"{sx} {sy}")
        return "M" + "L".join(steps) + "Z"

    rows = []
    total_points = 0
    for name, shape in projected:
        path = "".join(emit(ring) for ring in shape)
        total_points += sum(len(ring) for ring in shape)
        rows.append((key_for(name), name, path))

    keys = [k for k, _, _ in rows]
    if len(set(keys)) != len(keys):
        dupes = sorted({k for k in keys if keys.count(k) > 1})
        sys.exit(f"duplicate normalized keys: {dupes}")

    lines = []
    for key, name, path in rows:
        lines.append(f"  {{ name: '{key}', path: '{path}' }},")

    body = "\n".join(lines)
    out = f"""/**
 * Simplified district geometry for the cartogram map, written at build
 * time from geoBoundaries gbOpen CZE ADM2 (Public Domain,
 * www.geoboundaries.org, 77 districts). The outlines are projected to a
 * flat map, simplified with Douglas-Peucker, and rounded onto a 1000 by
 * {height} integer grid so the map keeps the same chunky pixel edge the rest
 * of the station wears. Names are normalized keys, the same shape
 * src/lib/districtNames.ts produces, so the cartogram can join a
 * districts.csv row to its outline without any network at runtime.
 */

/** The viewBox every path in this file is drawn on. */
export const CZECHIA_VIEW_BOX = '0 0 1000 {height}'

/** One district outline under its normalized name. */
export interface DistrictGeometry {{
  /** Normalized district name, the join key. */
  name: string
  /** SVG path data on CZECHIA_VIEW_BOX. */
  path: string
}}

/** All 77 districts, one path each. */
export const CZECHIA_DISTRICTS: readonly DistrictGeometry[] = [
{body}
]

/** Guard against a truncated or overgrown asset. */
export const CZECHIA_DISTRICT_COUNT = {len(rows)}
"""
    with open(out_path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        fh.write(out)
    print(f"wrote {out_path}: {len(rows)} districts, {total_points} points, {len(out)} bytes")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

/**
 * The district name join for the cartogram (Phase E5 map). districts.csv
 * and the map geometry come from two different publishers: the CSV spells
 * names in plain ASCII with Czech administrative prefixes intact, while
 * the geoBoundaries outlines ship proper diacritics and, for the nine
 * city and direction units, English wording. One normalizer turns both
 * sides into the same key, so the cartogram can shade an outline from a
 * CSV row without a hand maintained crosswalk table and without any
 * network at runtime.
 *
 * The rules, in order: strip combining marks, lowercase, collapse every
 * run of punctuation to a single space, drop leading capital prefixes
 * (only while tokens remain to drop, so Plzen mesto keeps its mesto),
 * and finally read a lone n as the word nad. The alias table maps the
 * nine English spellings onto the Czech wording the CSV uses.
 */

/** Leading tokens the Czech capital and city prefixes decompose to. */
const CAPITAL_PREFIXES: ReadonlySet<string> = new Set(['hl', 'hlavni', 'mesto', 'm'])

/**
 * geoBoundaries ships English names for the nine units the CSV spells in
 * Czech, keyed by the normalized English form.
 */
const ENGLISH_ALIASES: Readonly<Record<string, string>> = {
  prague: 'praha',
  'prague east': 'praha vychod',
  'prague west': 'praha zapad',
  'plzen city': 'plzen mesto',
  'plzen north': 'plzen sever',
  'plzen south': 'plzen jih',
  'brno city': 'brno mesto',
  'brno country': 'brno venkov',
  'ostrava city': 'ostrava mesto',
}

/** One district name reduced to its comparison key. */
export function normalizeDistrictName(name: string): string {
  const plain = name
    .normalize('NFD')
    .replace(/[̀-ͯ]/g, '')
    .toLowerCase()
  const tokens = plain.split(/[^a-z0-9]+/).filter((token) => token.length > 0)

  let start = 0
  while (start < tokens.length - 1 && CAPITAL_PREFIXES.has(tokens[start] ?? '')) {
    start += 1
  }

  return tokens
    .slice(start)
    .map((token) => (token === 'n' ? 'nad' : token))
    .join(' ')
}

/** The join key: the normalized name, then the English alias table. */
export function districtKey(name: string): string {
  const key = normalizeDistrictName(name)
  return ENGLISH_ALIASES[key] ?? key
}

+### Take a shock: shock simulator

 The verdict comes from one pure `verdictBand` function in `src/lib/verdict.ts`: five bands (critical, storm warning, watch, fair skies, clear) cut at 10, 30, 60, and 120 tenths of a month, with buffer depleted always reading Critical and no shortfall always reading Clear. +### Make a plan

+### Weather station visualization
 
 The forecast strip is a projection built from integer cents: a balance curve from the shocked buffer, a storm front at the landing month, and a landfall pin whose printed figure is the same headline runway the verdict badge shows. The horizon starts at 12 months, extends to the landfall month, and is capped at 120. Recorded average balances are drawn muted to the left of the projection as context only, beside the honesty note that the projection starts from buffer B, the mean of the last 6 recorded balances, never from the last recorded balance.
 
@@ -66,7 +66,7 @@ A band key prints all five verdict bands with their thresholds, lowest runway fi
 
 Instead of preset buttons, type the shock in plain language ("they lose their job, EI covers half, and the furnace dies next month").  An extension adds a district storm cartogram (77 districts) and a population rain gauge, both rendered from `public/data/engine/atlas.json`, precomputed on the five verdict bands by `scripts/engine/atlas.py`. -

"""Regenerate src/assets/czechia-districts.ts from the geoBoundaries release.

The cartogram map needs one SVG path per Czech district, and the app must
never fetch geometry at runtime, so the outlines are baked into a TypeScript
module that Vite bundles. This script is the build time step: it reads the
downloaded GeoJSON, projects it onto a flat map, simplifies it with
Douglas Peucker, rounds it onto an integer grid, and writes the module.

Source (public domain, fetched once when the geometry was committed):

  https://www.geoboundaries.org/api/current/gbOpen/CZE/ADM2/
  https://github.com/wmgeolab/geoBoundaries/raw/9469f09/releaseData/gbOpen/CZE/ADM2/geoBoundaries-CZE-ADM2_simplified.geojson

Download it with curl, then run:

  python3 scripts/map/build_district_geometry.py cze-adm2-simplified.geojson

The name rules live in src/lib/districtNames.ts, and
src/lib/districtNames.test.ts pins the join against data/tangerine/districts.csv,
so a regeneration that loses a district fails the TypeScript suite.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import math
import re
import sys
import unicodedata
from pathlib import Path

REPO = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]
DEFAULT_INPUT = Path(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else Path("cze-adm2-simplified.geojson")
DEFAULT_OUTPUT = REPO / "src" / "assets" / "czechia-districts.ts"

# Douglas Peucker tolerance in projected degrees. At the shipped scale one
# unit of the 1000 wide viewBox is under a pixel, and 0.0025 degrees is
# roughly half a pixel, so the simplification is invisible on screen.
TOLERANCE = 0.0025

VIEW_WIDTH = 1000
BORDER = 6.0

# geoBoundaries spells nine city and direction units in English while
# data/tangerine/districts.csv spells them in Czech. Keyed by the
# normalized English form, mirroring ENGLISH_ALIASES in districtNames.ts.
ALIASES = {
    "prague": "praha",
    "prague east": "praha vychod",
    "prague west": "praha zapad",
    "plzen city": "plzen mesto",
    "plzen north": "plzen sever",
    "plzen south": "plzen jih",
    "brno city": "brno mesto",
    "brno country": "brno venkov",
    "ostrava city": "ostrava mesto",
}

CAPITAL_PREFIXES = {"hl", "hlavni", "mesto", "m"}


def rings_of(geometry: dict) -> list:
    """Every ring of a Polygon or MultiPolygon feature."""
    if geometry["type"] == "Polygon":
        return geometry["coordinates"]
    rings: list = []
    for polygon in geometry["coordinates"]:
        rings.extend(polygon)
    return rings


def project(lon: float, lat: float, lat0: float, lon0: float) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Equirectangular with a cosine correction, y pointing down."""
    return ((lon - lon0) * math.cos(math.radians(lat0)), -lat)


def simplify(points: list, tolerance: float) -> list:
    """Iterative Douglas Peucker over a closed ring (first point repeated)."""
    if len(points) < 5:
        return points
    keep = [False] * len(points)
    keep[0] = keep[-1] = True
    stack = [(0, len(points) - 1)]
    tolerance_sq = tolerance * tolerance
    while stack:
        start, end = stack.pop()
        if end <= start + 1:
            continue
        ax, ay = points[start]
        bx, by = points[end]
        dx, dy = bx - ax, by - ay
        norm = dx * dx + dy * dy
        best = -1.0
        best_index = -1
        for index in range(start + 1, end):
            px, py = points[index]
            if norm == 0:
                distance = (px - ax) ** 2 + (py - ay) ** 2
            else:
                t = ((px - ax) * dx + (py - ay) * dy) / norm
                t = 0.0 if t < 0 else (1.0 if t > 1 else t)
                distance = (px - (ax + t * dx)) ** 2 + (py - (ay + t * dy)) ** 2
            if distance > best:
                best = distance
                best_index = index
        if best > tolerance_sq and best_index > 0:
            keep[best_index] = True
            stack.append((start, best_index))
            stack.append((best_index, end))
    return [point for point, flagged in zip(points, keep) if flagged]


def district_key(name: str) -> str:
    """The same join key src/lib/districtNames.ts produces."""
    plain = "".join(
        character

"""Regenerate src/assets/czechia-districts.ts from the geoBoundaries release.

The cartogram map needs one SVG path per Czech district, and the app must
never fetch geometry at runtime, so the outlines are baked into a TypeScript
module that Vite bundles. This script is the build time step: it reads the
downloaded GeoJSON, projects it onto a flat map, simplifies it with
Douglas Peucker, rounds it onto an integer grid, and writes the module.

Source (public domain, fetched once when the geometry was committed):

  https://www.geoboundaries.org/api/current/gbOpen/CZE/ADM2/
  https://github.com/wmgeolab/geoBoundaries/raw/9469f09/releaseData/gbOpen/CZE/ADM2/geoBoundaries-CZE-ADM2_simplified.geojson

Download it with curl, then run:

  python3 scripts/map/build_district_geometry.py cze-adm2-simplified.geojson

The name rules live in src/lib/districtNames.ts, and
src/lib/districtNames.test.ts pins the join against data/tangerine/districts.csv,
so a regeneration that loses a district fails the TypeScript suite.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import math
import re
import sys
import unicodedata
from pathlib import Path

REPO = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]
DEFAULT_INPUT = Path(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else Path("cze-adm2-simplified.geojson")
DEFAULT_OUTPUT = REPO / "src" / "assets" / "czechia-districts.ts"

# Douglas Peucker tolerance in projected degrees. At the shipped scale one
# unit of the 1000 wide viewBox is under a pixel, and 0.0025 degrees is
# roughly half a pixel, so the simplification is invisible on screen.
TOLERANCE = 0.0025

VIEW_WIDTH = 1000
BORDER = 6.0

# geoBoundaries spells nine city and direction units in English while
# data/tangerine/districts.csv spells them in Czech. Keyed by the
# normalized English form, mirroring ENGLISH_ALIASES in districtNames.ts.
ALIASES = {
    "prague": "praha",
    "prague east": "praha vychod",
    "prague west": "praha zapad",
    "plzen city": "plzen mesto",
    "plzen north": "plzen sever",
    "plzen south": "plzen jih",
    "brno city": "brno mesto",
    "brno country": "brno venkov",
    "ostrava city": "ostrava mesto",
}

CAPITAL_PREFIXES = {"hl", "hlavni", "mesto", "m"}


def rings_of(geometry: dict) -> list:
    """Every ring of a Polygon or MultiPolygon feature."""
    if geometry["type"] == "Polygon":
        return geometry["coordinates"]
    rings: list = []
    for polygon in geometry["coordinates"]:
        rings.extend(polygon)
    return rings


def project(lon: float, lat: float, lat0: float, lon0: float) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Equirectangular with a cosine correction, y pointing down."""
    return ((lon - lon0) * math.cos(math.radians(lat0)), -lat)


def simplify(points: list, tolerance: float) -> list:
    """Iterative Douglas Peucker over a closed ring (first point repeated)."""
    if len(points) < 5:
        return points
    keep = [False] * len(points)
    keep[0] = keep[-1] = True
    stack = [(0, len(points) - 1)]
    tolerance_sq = tolerance * tolerance
    while stack:
        start, end = stack.pop()
        if end <= start + 1:
            continue
        ax, ay = points[start]
        bx, by = points[end]
        dx, dy = bx - ax, by - ay
        norm = dx * dx + dy * dy
        best = -1.0
        best_index = -1
        for index in range(start + 1, end):
            px, py = points[index]
            if norm == 0:
                distance = (px - ax) ** 2 + (py - ay) ** 2
            else:
                t = ((px - ax) * dx + (py - ay) * dy) / norm
                t = 0.0 if t < 0 else (1.0 if t > 1 else t)
                distance = (px - (ax + t * dx)) ** 2 + (py - (ay + t * dy)) ** 2
            if distance > best:
                best = distance
                best_index = index
        if best > tolerance_sq and best_index > 0:
            keep[best_index] = True
            stack.append((start, best_index))
            stack.append((best_index, end))
    return [point for point, flagged in zip(points, keep) if flagged]

    """The same join key src/lib/districtNames.ts produces."""
    plain = "".join(
        character

        if not unicodedata.combining(character)

        start += 1
    key = " ".join(token for token in tokens[start:] if token != "n" or True)
    key = " ".join("nad" if token == "n" else token for token in tokens[start:])
    return ALIASES.get(key, key)

    latitudes: list[float] = []
    longitudes: list[float] = []

    lon0 = (min(longitudes) + max(longitudes)) / 2

    projected: list[tuple[str, list[list[tuple[float, float]]]]] = []

            points = [project(lon, lat, lat0, lon0) for lon, lat in ring]

            if len(points) >= 4:
                shape.append(points)
        projected.append((feature["properties"]["shapeName"], shape))

    xs = [x for _, shape in projected for ring in shape for x, _ in ring]
    ys = [y for _, shape in projected for ring in shape for _, y in ring]
    min_x, max_x = min(xs), max(xs)
    min_y, max_y = min(ys), max(ys)

    span_x = max_x - min_x
    span_y = max_y - min_y
    height = round(VIEW_WIDTH * span_y / span_x)
    scale = (VIEW_WIDTH - 2 * BORDER) / span_x

        steps = [
            f"{round((x - min_x) * scale + BORDER)} {round((y - min_y) * scale + BORDER)}"
            for x, y in ring

        return "M" + "L".join(steps) + "Z"

    rows: list[tuple[str, str]] = []
    points_total = 0

        path = "".join(emit(ring) for ring in shape)
        points_total += sum(len(ring) for ring in shape)
        rows.append((district_key(name), path))

    keys = [key for key, _ in rows]
    duplicates = sorted({key for key in keys if keys.count(key) > 1})
    if duplicates:
        raise SystemExit(f"duplicate normalized keys: {duplicates}")

    body = "\n".join(f"  {{ name: '{key}', path: '{path}' }}," for key, path in rows)
    module = f"""/**
 * Simplified district geometry for the cartogram map, written by
 * scripts/map/build_district_geometry.py from geoBoundaries gbOpen
 * CZE ADM2 (Public Domain, www.geoboundaries.org, 77 districts). The
 * outlines are projected to a flat map, simplified with Douglas
 * Peucker, and rounded onto a 1000 by {height} integer grid so the map
 * keeps the same chunky pixel edge the rest of the station wears.
 * Names are normalized keys, the same shape src/lib/districtNames.ts
 * produces, so the cartogram joins a districts.csv row to its outline
 * with no network at runtime.
 */

/** The viewBox every path in this file is drawn on. */
export const CZECHIA_VIEW_BOX = '0 0 1000 {height}'

/** One district outline under its normalized name. */
export interface DistrictGeometry {{
  /** Normalized district name, the join key. */
  name: string
  /** SVG path data on CZECHIA_VIEW_BOX. */
  path: string
}}

/** All 77 districts, one path each. */
export const CZECHIA_DISTRICTS: readonly DistrictGeometry[] = [

export const CZECHIA_DISTRICT_COUNT = {len(rows)}

    DEFAULT_OUTPUT.write_text(module, encoding="utf-8")

### Stage 4: cartogram as a real map

- **Source:** geoBoundaries **gbOpen CZE ADM2**, license **Public Domain**, 77 units, `boundaryCanonical: District`.
  API: `https://www.geoboundaries.org/api/current/gbOpen/CZE/ADM2/`
  File: `https://github.com/wmgeolab/geoBoundaries/raw/9469f09/releaseData/gbOpen/CZE/ADM2/geoBoundaries-CZE-ADM2_simplified.geojson`
- **Pipeline:** equirectangular projection with cos(lat) correction → Douglas-Peucker at 0.0025° (≈0.5 viewBox unit) → integer rounding on a `0 0 1000 572` grid (which is what gives the map the same chunky edge as the rest of the station) → `src/assets/czechia-districts.ts`.
- **Final size:** **78,085 bytes** (74,299 B of path data), 9,381 points, 77 paths. Well under the ~150 KB target. Generator committed at `scripts/map/build_district_geometry.py`; re-running it reproduces the committed body byte for byte.
- **Name match: 77/77, 0 unmatched, 0 orphan outlines.** Normalizer strips diacritics, collapses punctuation, drops leading `hl / hlavni / mesto / m` prefixes (`Hl.m. Praha` and `Hlavní město Praha` → `praha`), reads a lone `n` as `nad` (`Jablonec n. Nisou`), and an alias table maps the nine English geometry names (`Prague-East`, `Plzeň-City`, `Brno-Country`, `Ostrava-City` …) onto the CSV wording. Pinned permanently by `src/lib/districtNames.test.ts`, which reads `data/tangerine/districts.csv` and asserts every row joins and every outline is claimed. **Tile fallback is implemented and tested** (mixed fixture: 2 paths + 1 tile + the fallback legend sentence), just never triggered by shipped data.

A district with no counts takes **no shade** (white) so absent data never reads as a safe zero.
